game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I love the game but it has some quirks.
1. Like some others, I believe that 'conflicting data chunks' should be revisable after entry pending new evidence.  The 'Test Case' has two personality traits that could both be true... or neither.  You have to choose one.
2. Is that... a bug?  Further into Test Case you need to find the full name of a Person of Interest.  I spent 10 minutes digging and digging through all available documents and found ONE listing of the name (immediately, actually) but it wasn't highlighted as a valid and usable Data Chunk.  Literally NOTHING else anywhere on this guy's name.  (Either I hardcore dumbed it up here or there's a bug regarding this Data Chunk.)
3. Restrictive Data Chunk gathering.  I recognized/found quite a bit of relevant data in documents but wasn't able to enter/drag-drop it as a Data Chunk into the appropriate Person of Interest's file... just because it didn't want me to worry about that yet?

Of course, I was just under an hour into the game and -mostly- (I think?) through the first 'Test' Case so issue #3 may just be a 'beginner' or tutorial-ish feature as it coaxes you into learning how to play without need of a cut-and-dry tutorial.  Overall, I say this game is definitely worth giving a try if you enjoy modern mysteries and actively uncovering the story for yourself.

I've spent almost 3 hours on the game at the time of writing and intend on going through it doing different things the next time and see what happens. Its highly unnerving and brilliant and the soundtrack is well worth getting as the soundtrack is one of my absolute favourites. There is literraly one stage in the game where you get hacked and I thought my actual laptop was getting hacked it was done that well. The story line is brilliant and I'm hoping there will be a sequel or second season.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h3][i]“War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]


Even if you haven't read anything by George Orwell, you've probably heard about 1984. The dystopia the author foresaw has undoubtedly materialized in the modern world, as most readers of the book like to point out. This assertion is without doubt true; even if you only use the internet for personal purposes, there are still a lot of data crumbs left behind. You can never be certain if someone is keeping an eye on your every online move, whether it be a post about a recent vacation, a comment made on a forum, or the address you use to sign emails. 
This is precisely what Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You promises: it is a game about a reality that nobody wants to face but that hangs in the air.

[h3][i]“The consequences of every act are included in the act itself.”[/i] - George Orwell[/h3]

The game takes place in the capital of a fictional country called The Nation, where on April 12th, 2017, a terrorist attack occurs: a bomb detonates in the famous Freedom Plaza, destroying a statue and killing several people. At the same time, the police receive a note containing the first three stanzas of a German folk song called The Thoughts are Free.

In 2012, The Party, a paternalistic government that leads The Nation, passed the Safety Bill, which gave the government complete freedom over citizens' personal data and the ability to spy on them using a surveillance system called Orwell. This is where your involvement with The Nation begins.
You are the first person who has been selected to be an investigator - a citizen outside of The Nation, who will use Orwell to uncover as much data about a person as possible. You are being accompanied by an Advisor, who will connect you to the authorities. 

The plot is essentially a classic detective whodunit story told in five chapters; throughout the game, multiple suspects will emerge, and your job will be to determine each person's involvement and, in the end, find the perpetrator(s) - or is it?
The aforementioned data (which the game refers to as datachucks) gathering is the game's main essence and gameplay mechanic - you have access to a wide range of websites, phones, e-mail addresses, and even computers, where you must find information related to your lead. This isn't a difficult task because the game highlights them in blue or yellow; the latter indicates a data collision, and you must determine which is the correct data.

A few things should be kept in mind with this mechanic: first, it is completely irreversible - once you upload something in the system, there is no way to change it, and the story will proceed accordingly; second, you do not need to upload every possible datachunk - at first, the game forces you to do this, but later you must be careful what you upload; and third, the game is actually a choose-your-own-adventure with a detective façade - given that there are multiple endings, your choices will have a heavy impact on the story.

Orwell's strength is the moral uncertainty it contains. Players will have to weigh the pros and cons of sharing new information with the people they're investigating versus keeping it to themselves as they gather additional evidence. Because of this, players will feel more invested in the game and more emotionally connected to their choices.

[h3][i]“But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]

One of the game's greatest strengths is its immersive and atmospheric presentation. The dark and minimalist art style, combined with a haunting original soundtrack, sets the perfect tone for an oppressive world governed by The Party. The user interface is sleek and intuitive, allowing easy navigation of the vast amount of information at your disposal. Towards the end of the game, the interface will get much more crowded; however, the game displays a red icon next to a document where new data chunks can be found. Furthermore, the game's soundtrack perfectly complements the dystopian atmosphere, with haunting melodies and industrial beats that immerse players in the world of surveillance and control. 

Orwell does, however, have a few minor flaws. As the investigation progresses through a series of data-mining tasks, the gameplay can feel slow at times. Some players, particularly those who prefer more action-oriented experiences, may find these moments tedious. Furthermore, while the game encourages players to take different paths, the overall impact of your choices on the narrative can feel somewhat limited, leaving some room for a more dynamic and personalized experience unexplored.
The length of the game is another aspect of the experience that could be improved. The story is interesting and the decisions are weighty, yet the game is over in a matter of hours and it left me craving for more. The game's depth of topic and potential for replay may have benefited from more content or branching routes.



[h3][i]“Freedom is the freedom to say that two plus two make four. If that is granted, all else follows.”[/i]
 - George Orwell[/h3]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a fascinating and unsettling adventure that delves into the moral issues raised by omniscient monitoring and the misuse of authority. A standout in the narrative-driven genre, thanks to its engaging tale, accessible gameplay, and morally weighty choices. Even though it's not particularly long and has a few weaker points, it's a must-play if you enjoy engaging stories set in dystopian futures.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In the wake of a recent bombing, someone needs to be tasked to help investigate the suspected bombers. That someone is you. You are in charge of what goes in the system and what doesn't. But is there more to it? Is there a group planning it all together, or just one person? Do you paint them as terrorists or do you leave out enough information to show them as innocent?

[h1]Welcome to Orwell[/h1]
Orwell is one of those stories that is best to go blind in, since it is the most effective the first time. Hearing or seeing anything that is related to the main story, especially the end, ruins how you would play. But why? You are playing yourself, a new recruit of a programed named Orwell tasked to investigate suspicious people regarding the recent bombing. Through, which I wished happened more, a cutscene perfectly showing why and what this game is with only visuals. If you read 1984 Orwell is similar to how the government watches their people as it was influenced from George Orwell's books.

[h1]Datachunk Uploaded[/h1]
Down to it's core, you only read highlighted items, or datachunks, and dragging them to profiles for uploading. But there is much more if you are willing. Datachunks are meant to be evaluated, is this noteworthy to put on someone's profile? Do you purposefully make someone look worse or better? Should you upload every little thing? The game tried to put you in this mindset by your supervisor's comments and by conflicting datachunks (represented by a yellow highlight) to show you can't upload every little thing. Of course, there are datachunks needed to continue. Most of the time it is very apparent the datachunk is needed as it gives something new you can look through, solve a conflicting datachunk, or a sound cue picks up. This is all combined to represent how you view the situation. How you view the people you were tasked to investigate. How you have an influence on how their life will go after Orwell injected you into their lives. Sure, they do make their own decisions, but you have the power to have them forever be seen as a threat by the government.

Your first playthrough is key. It is how you would react in this situation, not how some character would. You do not know anything except what you gather. All other playthroughs after that is to see what could have happened if you did something differently. Anything you know about the main storyline ruins how you make decisions in the game. So I do recommend knowing as little as possible to get the most out of it.

I suppose Orwell is too easy. You have a supervisor meant to guide you, not only in Orwell but to guide your progress through the main storyline. It is very easy to just scroll down till you see phrases or words highlighted. Trying to find conflicting datachunks quickly to get past. While there is nothing stopping you, Orwell does try to encourage you to read. The many articles and websites you visit build the world as you continually gain access. In a way, the people you investigate brings you into the world as you unknowingly destroy theirs each datachunk at a time. There has been arguments about taking away the automatic highlighting, as why should you be hired if they have a system that does it, but there is too much that one can assume is needed. It could easily become entering random phrases or words till you get it right. So this way of highlighting does take away this confusion of what is and isn't noteworthy in a wall of text or conversations.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
There's limited sounds to Orwell, having background music and computer sounds. The background soundtrack never really changes until something notewrothy and important comes into view. While computer sounds symbolizes actions, such as a sound of a phone for a phone call and a click as datachunks are being entered.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
While you do stare at a screen of your computer, Orwell has an interesting style when it comes to pictures. They build people with polygons. This gives an interesting visual that pops out when surrounded by text and brightening up the screen. The opening cutscene is one of the places that does not primarily showcase this style, going for more of an shaded outline. While the visuals are minimal, it does look appealing.

[h1]Performance[/h1]
Orwell easily runs well. Only having a few seconds of loading in the beginning of each chapter to load everything. There also seems to be a rare bug, not allowing the player to drag or view the preview of the datachunk. Thankfully, the datachunk is not needed to continue with the story, as it persists through the save, so it may only bother those who view it as an important datachunk to include in a profile.

[h1]Revisiting Orwell[/h1]
As said before, Orwell thrives on the first playthrough. After that, you know what's going to happen. You know what choices affects those you were assigned to. That first playthrough may be remembered as you replay, but so everthing major to the story. This is where you should look up guides as more playthroughs are solely for achievements that were off of the course you took. There are a total of three offical endings, all having subtle changed down the road. There's not much replayability but to see the difference the decisions have on the suspects.

[h1]Report[/h1]
+ Art style
+ Convincing characters; can easily be viewed as real people
+ Compelling story

+/- Your choice to see the world of Orwell
+/- Can be seen as constantly holding your hand

- The phone calls and texts are either too slow or too fast. You have to activate the certain call/text for it to start, breaking immersion since no one will wait till you come into the picture. If you are fast enough you can get two calls or texts (or a combination of the two) at the same time since you are likely to look at something else during other playthroughs. 

Orwell is one of those must play games. With the close hitting theme that may soon become reality. With all chapters released, you can easily have 2-3 hours of gamethrough per playthrough depending on how you choose to play. Orwell shows that you are being watched in some ways, even now, and that even you won't have the best interest for others if they have the possibility to be threats to society. Do not be afraid of going into Orwell this late, as I have and I was able to still get the most out of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Fantastic game, I can't praise it enough. Solid story, solid characters and character progression, appealing art style, and perfect general pacing. The soundtrack, works perfectly for it- being that it's essentially a solid, subtle repeat throughout the entire game really makes those times where it picks up stand out and feel that much more important.  I really, really hope to see more from this company. And, admittedly, would love it if this premise is revisited in some way. This is the best game I've played in a long, long time. Exactly what I've been looking for. I just couldn't stop playing. I'm kind of sad that I've completely finished it. 

Issues; 
Some of the dialogue becomes a bit broken depending on your choices. Oftentimes Symes and Delacroix mentioned information that I'd intentionally not given them, later on in the story. This only really becomes noticeable on replay-but it could be worked on. Nothing like this will ever be perfect--I'm never going to seriously complain about a choice game having little issues like this. There's just too much that would have to go into a game with so many variants it to make it possible. 
There were a few lingering spelling/grammatical errors, which, given the nature of the game (Internet, instant messaging/texting), didn't really bother me all that much. (Such as Harrison tried to "fell" instead of flee.) I see these things on real articles, it's no different.
There are some bugs present, but, they're clearly being revised and, honestly, aren't game-breaking at this point.

My personal ideas; I believe there could be a little work done on the pacing of the listener- real-time DOES make it all that much more immersive, but, when it comes to replayabilty, and just the general idea of it most likely having an adult player-base, who may only have an hour or so to play before going back to their day-to-day, I feel like there should be...maybe an additional option in the settings to modify speed or..something? It's easier, and more fulfilling to put a game down for a session if you feel you were able to hit a certain level of 'achievement.' You know, the pleasure centers of the brain and all. Maybe if it were simply a more fluid letter-by-letter or syllabalic instead of by completion of a word? I don't know. 
The only other thing I could possibly suggest, would be for, if ever this title is revisited or turned into a 'series' of sorts, that it be a little more flexible? The ability to freely investigate more than is necessary--even additional people. Perhaps just in a casual sense aside from the story, since there is a necessary feeling of a 'time pinch' in the game itself. I think a lot of the audience are people like me who just like to dig, so the chance to just..index on a larger scale would be quite entertaining. 
And, lastly, the ability to generate more datachunks? This could be messy territory, though. I think this would fall into the 'would require too much forethought to ever be possible' category, but it's an idea nontheless. The system is automated, clearly, but, the evaluator should have an option to deem other things appropriate for investigation. I know there were a few things that I would have loved to have flagged that just weren't an option.

My apologies, I'm just VERY excited and passionate about this title. Guys, play it!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Running on PopOS Linux (and this game has a linux client)... crashed on activating the first achievement.

Which is about the time I was ready to walk away from the game anyway.

Interesting idea, and definitely innovative as far as visual novels go, but that's all this is... another visual novel masquerading as an adventure game. You don't have to play hours and hours of this to figure out that your choices might provide some slight deviations in the story, but ultimately it's a very narrow path.

There is no adventure here, there are no puzzles.

The interactivity involves dragging across auto-highlighted data you "discover" to build a profile, as well as other profiles connecting to your primary suspect... all from static articles/reports/etc. and active chat sessions that you monitor. No reading through and figuring out what data has actual value the way it is done in the real world. You can read it all, but that isn't really necessary... just skim and speed click your way ahead and you can push the story forward. Feel like you're stuck, something that hasn't been done will remain "starred", so you can go back to that article or whatever and the game will what to do.

Policing/Defense/Military/Whatever-Agency surveillance staff that perform these profile building intelligence jobs and put together these profiles... it's an interesting concept that could have been turned into a fascinating text heavy game that required minimal computing resources or HDD footprint... but the NPC that is effectively your handler guides you the whole way, further holding your hand on top of the highlighted text/data that tells you that you can do something.

That completely kills any mental engagement on a gaming level. You are simply a consumer of a story, which is fine... but that's not a game. That's an interactive short story, or an animated slide show/film/something... not a game.

Steam needs to enforce some sort of standard for the tags to many of these types of "games"... your choices don't really matter here. And a politically themed visual novel that constantly tells you and shows you what to do... that does not qualify as being a "sim". You do not need to "think" when you play Orwell, just obey orders and click where you are allowed to click... you could almost mistake it for a poetic and poignant Orwellian statement on its own existence as a "game"...  but it's not. It really is not.

review_text_raw:
I've only played one case. Maybe it gets better but I already hate it. This is a game that saw [i]Papers Please[/i] and a Telltale game and thought: these should be one thing. They shouldn't. It wants to have the humanism of a game that is mostly just a postmodern exploration of character ([i]Her Story, Analogue: A Hate Story[/i]), but it also wants you to make binary data choices on which set of data to pass on to your superior without being given enough information to know how it will be interpreted.

[i]Papers Please[/i] presents very clear outcomes for the majority of your choices and the moral weight they have and gives a context for why a choice must be made anyway.  By presenting the status quo of a job which you must do for a family who could starve, the game allows for depth of story, a context for why things must be as they are and real stakes for the choices that are made.

Telltale games often don't pre-empt the outcomes of your choices, but often these choices are superfluous because what matters is the character drama. But the thing is that the games sensationalize these choices and make them feel like they could matter, even when they don't. This character could die instead of this one, you might find out a different set of information, but the structure of the story and the characters' movement through it remains intact. 

When you mash them up what you get is a completely unnuanced yes-no/good-bad moral choice system ala Fable in a world that resembles the real one too closely for that to not be cringe-worthy. Only the binary isn't good/bad because as someone who is already spying on someone and potentially ruining their life just to test if you can get access to the next document by adding chunks that seem only tangentially related but will be interpreted as reason to call the police, you're always bad. And if that's what the game's political critique boils down to, then I got it. Thumbs up.

"Are they really terrorists?" the game's description asks. And the answer is no. I could have guessed that from the bugged out clip following her getting on a bus that only played the second time I started a new game because the first one I hit a dead end and had no choice but to just start adding data at random hoping something would trigger only to have to google and find out it was a known bug and I just had to restart from the start. So thanks, I hate it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The game advertises itself as a Big Brother simulator, but it doesn't [i]quite[/i] reach that level of depth and intrigue that kind of premise could reach.

However, I don't think Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You isn't a bad game at all. I think it's definitely a concept that is executed well. You play as an investigator who's collecting information on a variety of people through public channels, such as social media outlets, and private channels such as one's email. These pieces of information are used as evidence to solve the crime you're assigned to.

There is some decision-making in the game and it was interesting to see how the conversation changes between characters after performing certain actions. There are a couple of routes to take, but ultimately, the resolution is relatively the same. I don't mind this that much, and I honestly think true choice games are difficult to make, unless you have the resources as a studio.

However, the main element I found to be lacking was the story; it was rather light. There are a few tense moments in the story, but overall, it seemed like the writers decided on a safer route. I was expecting somewhat darker and more philosophical themes to be used in the game. They are touched upon lightly, but not expanded to play any significant role. Given the premise, there's a whole world of deep possibilities that could be played out, but the writing just scratches the surface of this. In the end, I found myself wanting a little more out of the game.

All in all, the game was less than satisfactory for me and I'd give it a neutral rating, if I could. If you're new to the whole 'mass surveillance' idea and want to see a taste of what a game could do with that idea, then sure, go play this. But if you want something deeper, this isn't quite it.

Side note: I also bought and played the DLC and it's just more of the same, in my opinion.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Worth it? Yes. DLC? Yes. Get it on sale? Probably, but it's worth the price if you have disposable income.
I really enjoyed playing Orwell and its DLC. Here's a bullet point of stuff I think is worth knowing before you buy!

-Plot/characters are realistic in a way that would normally be mundane on their own, but this game makes it somehow feel exceptional enough to make the story worth investing in. I think this grounding to reality did a good service by this game's namesake to express the urgency and importance of privacy and compassion, IRL and online.

-Easy to navigate UI, text is usually easy to read. The news articles' text is a bit thin, but if you have a big monitory/screen it probably won't be a problem. And you typically don't need to read every word on each website and email anyway.

-Markers for unread/unused/new "datachunks" that make going back through old info much less tedious.

-Easy to immerse in because you don't have to pretend to be someone you're not to fit yourself into the world of the game. It does feel like a job, but one that has wild stuff happening and your only way to know about it is through the job. Making the player curious is really important for mystery/puzzle/investigative games, and this game did a 7/10 job with that.

-While it does take effort to make sure you're keeping up with all the info, and making sure you're not wasting resources on unimportant info; it's not overly difficult. it's not necessarily easy (the first time around), but it won't make you feel stupid if you do struggle.

-The general concept of this game is so cool to me, I wish there were a lot more games like this.

-This game is much more accessible to people who have little in-depth experience with technology. It does all the technical "hacker" type work for you, and just lets you dig through people's lives unburdened. I don't really care about all the technical stuff involved in hacking & the like, so this was a huge win for me. A game like this can flop because of poorly executed, insanely difficult to comprehend, or super unrealistic hacking mechanics; so Orwell pretty much bypassed that while still making you feel like you're putting the pieces together yourself. (As long as you don't think too hard about it, anyway.)

-It puts you in a position of being the bad guy in a situation that makes you think, "This could literally be happening IRL and I wouldn't know." This game will give you a lot to think about even after you're done playing. 

-There is an issue that happened to me twice, where I technically soft locked myself in the game, and was unable to find any answers through walkthroughs/watching others play the game. So be prepared to be very diligent when uploading info when you are not racing the clock, and don't log out for the day until you're absolutely certain you've nabbed all the important info you might need.

-This game is honestly a bit short for the sheer amount of story and world-building information available in it. I think the game should have given you more time to explore and given more options for gathering info before forcing the plot to continue, even if not all of the info is used. It holds your hand too much, but not outright.

-Overall, my biggest issues with this game have to be the fact that you can't skip or pause chats or phone calls you're observing, and it moves so fast at certain points that you don't have time to process the information you're gathering to learn about the world/characters/story. My favorite parts of this game are really just the overall experience of playing it, and the execution of concept being very clear and deliberate.

It does feel like a job, but one that has wild stuff happening and your only way to know about it is through the job. Making the player curious is really important for mystery/puzzle/investigative games, and this game did a 7/10 job with that. -While it does take effort to make sure you're keeping up with all the info, and making sure you're not wasting resources on unimportant info; it's not overly difficult. it's not necessarily easy (the first time around), but it won't make you feel stupid if you do struggle. -The general concept of this game is so cool to me, I wish there were a lot more games like this. -This game is much more accessible to people who have little in-depth experience with technology. It does all the technical "hacker" type work for you, and just lets you dig through people's lives unburdened. I don't really care about all the technical stuff involved in hacking & the like, so this was a huge win for me. A game like this can flop because of poorly executed, insanely difficult to comprehend, or super unrealistic hacking mechanics; so Orwell pretty much bypassed that while still making you feel like you're putting the pieces together yourself. (As long as you don't think too hard about it, anyway.) -It puts you in a position of being the bad guy in a situation that makes you think, "This could literally be happening IRL and I wouldn't know." This game will give you a lot to think about even after you're done playing. -There is an issue that happened to me twice, where I technically soft locked myself in the game, and was unable to find any answers through walkthroughs/watching others play the game. So be prepared to be very diligent when uploading info when you are not racing the clock, and don't log out for the day until you're absolutely certain you've nabbed all the important info you might need. -This game is honestly a bit short for the sheer amount of story and world-building information available in it. I think the game should have given you more time to explore and given more options for gathering info before forcing the plot to continue, even if not all of the info is used. It holds your hand too much, but not outright. -Overall, my biggest issues with this game have to be the fact that you can't skip or pause chats or phone calls you're observing, and it moves so fast at certain points that you don't have time to process the information you're gathering to learn about the world/characters/story. My favorite parts of this game are really just the overall experience of playing it, and the execution of concept being very clear and deliberate.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Whoa! What a morally complex game! I've spent so much time thinking about some decisions. Some i did not think through, some turned out pretty well! It was great piecing all the information together and even if i missed some stuff, i'd say i've done a pretty decent job.

Spoiler warnings ahead.

What is right in this game? I honestly have no idea. The Orwell system did spy a lot on it's citizens (if only them lol), however if graphs are to be believed, the safety did increase and quite a lot. I even prevented one bombing and saved some lives!

Even if that bombing was in the end meant to fight the corrupted attempts at surveillance - it was only partially justified. Did the ends justify the means? It's easy to say these few sacrifices of people through bombings might have been justified.

However, as an investigator, it molded my first perception of The Thought group in a negative view. But then, without the hacker and other people's involvement would i (or for that matter anyone) be able to expose the unethical use of surveillance?

Who knows. But then, it seemed like Abraham wasn't this ''great hero'' either. He was paranoic of living in that Germany town, because everyone knew someone? I did not get his motivations there.
He even left his loving family - his wife and daughter who were quite deeply affected by that, so he can preach on university about thoughts being free? He also got traumatised in that Rhosen tech company, after he saw the failures of the earlier Orwell version, yet he became involved and sped up the process.

If he was so ''understanding'' of ethics and thoughts being free, i'm sure he would've noticed that the other employers did not care about them.
Then he gave upgrade to Orwell and was surprised that they did workarounds for his ethical codexes. It seems like his own thoughts weren't free in the first place and his decisions were quite irrational, motivated by fear.

Honestly, he and Thought members, Delacroix and likely other higher ups, many other people and finally me as investigator were partially to blame. I feel like a decent amount of people were truly in fault.

ALSO, i think if i didn't stop that bomb, the diplomatic talks abroad would have not worked. I mean sure, they were in part planned to keep Orwell on working, but it also seems like the Nation was doing some charitable actions in other countries too.

At first i was supportive of Orwell system, howere the issue was with the higher ups being unethical jerks - with the advisor guy Symes being actually really nice guy and with nice family. I was glad he made it out safe out of his house and i hope he could live his life somewhat normally afterwards.

If the Delacroix and perhaps others would have been more decent human beings and actually did have a solid ethical codex, that is well reviewed scientifically, then i believe Orwell could had been actually a successful surveillance system with way better results.

In the first half of the game i was really surprised of how well the system worked. I did stop the third bombing after all. It definitely could get some improvements, like possibility of retracing data (due to new informations) and retracing arrests (i felt bad for some of them and, based on achievements, i might've arrested one or more people unjustly).

This game gave me interesting insight into surveillance. With more twixes and solid, peer reviewed codex - that one has to strictly abide to, i believe this could work much better. It already did, based on the decreasing crime rates - i'm 100% sure it had caught many criminals off guard, since i was able to infiltrate the devices of the head of security herself.

MAN! What a game! I certainly did not expect much from it, but it had blown my expectations! Honestly i think it's going to land in my favourites. Excellent game.

I believe the game posed some really morally gray views. It's hard for me to say that one person / side is right and others wrong. I did not expect such complexity and it kind of reminds me of Attack on Titan moral dilemmas. It feels like each approach has it's downsides, but also justifications and i love that. In the end there might be no one single right choice to make. Instead it may be up to our egos and making the choice we would regret the least.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Excellent game.

To those who know the references and like the source material this game is based off of, this is perhaps the best Big Brother/Orwellian Surveillance system simulator I've seen so far, and is well worth the price its asking for. 

Fans of Papers, Please will probably enjoy this game just as much. Except instead of being the Border Crossing Guard, think of yourself as the Investigator for their Surveillance Corps.

Its a short game, sure, you can beat it once probably within 4 hours, but it does have some replayability (plus the fact that there is no hard save points, the game constantly saves after everything you do with no way of going back outside of making a new profile, so it forces you to choose wisely). To me, the shortness is forgiveable for how much this game costs (which isn't much).

The writing is amazing for it being a game with only written dialogue, the characters feel real and individual and you're the spider trying to weave out the web of how they fit into the plot that's going on. It also does a great job of getting you into the role of being an Investigator of a secret service public spying agency, you feel as if you're in the game just as much as any of them at times.

The art style is consistent and works for the game that this is, but IMO they could have had clear photos and models and you would have had the same game, this style merely gives it a more individual feel rather than it being like any other game like this.

The gameplay is simple, but great if you're into investigative puzzle-solving.

The music is very good for eliciting responses and making you feel certain emotions at particular times, as its supposed to, though IMO it moves a little too fast at times in transitions. You're often left with an abrupt music cue and wondering "What the hell, what did I just find?" before you can properly read what found. But otherwise its good.

Only encountered one bug at the very end of the game where it froze and looped the last second or two of the music track I was listening to, and I had to exit out with alt-tab, but I had beaten the playthrough by that point so it wasn't a huge deal.

All and all, a great game for the price its asking for, and if you're a fan of the type of genre this is.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Thoughts[/h1]

So let start off with saying I purchased the full game after playing the demo, looking back the demo actually offers everything that you would find in the main game so I would highly suggest playing the demo before making a purchase and understand that the gameplay isnt any different.

The premise of the game is to locate pertinent information about certain suspects in response to a terror attack, the information is uploaded to a system for your superior to review. The superior talks to pretty much every time you upload something, questioning the information and how it can be used against them.  The communication is totally one way and unfortunately because of the limited information you can upload sometimes it is taken very much out of context. e.g. someone was torturing someone else with muffins…. Uploading this to the system and the superior freaked out saying this person needs investigating because they like to torture people.  Hmm, I get that is the game design but yeah it’s a bit bizarre.

I use the term locate here very loosely because the game essentially spoon feeds you documents, links and webpages that contains the important information, the task at hand is to determine if the information is actually useful or not.  Every now and then you get some information which conflicts and you have to upload just one piece of information however this type of interaction doesn’t happen that often which is a shame.

I also didn’t like how the story abruptly ended, it wasn’t obvious in any way that if I upload this bit of information the game would finish.  I was taken completely by surprise and I understand there are multiple endings available but the choice just wasn’t obvious.

Despite playing the demo I still assumed the game would offer a lot more detective work later on, I assumed that I would need to locate web pages, search people and scan the documents but no.  The system finds everything and then sends you it gift tied in a little star shaped parcel.  All you do is drag and drop blue text to the box on the left and occasionally choose between one bit of yellow text and another bit of yellow text.

Overall I think this game offers great potential but it falls down with its boring repetitive gameplay that require zero thought or analysis.  If you are wanting a detective text based game look at Hacknet, for me that that is far superior to this as its on you to find and locate the information rather than it being spoon fed to you.

So, where to get started ... Orwell was one of  the many games in my steam library collecting dust because I got it at some point but never got around to actually playing it. I picked it first over other games as I just started reading a book called '1984' by George Orwell. For anyone who enjoyed the book it's worth checking out the game. Although the book has a much better story in my opinion and if you enjoyed the game you really should check it out.

It took me about 5 hours for my first run. For me it was quite  an immersive experience and the game does a really good job at making you feel at the center of the plot. The story is not linear and the choices you make do feel like they actually matter unlike the old fallout games.  It was an interesting experience, but at some points the gameplay did hinder you with an obtrusive dialogue of your 'advisor', but not to the point if it becoming annoying.

To summarize without spoiling, it's about the future and ethics of our civilization and how we'll deal with privacy. Just as the book did, but in a simply numbed down version. The game is therefor not perfect, it lacked some depth in certain parts of the story. But the fact that you can go and play the game again will make the second time playing a complete different experience as you can now advance with knowledge of your previous playthrough which makes up for it.

~~==~~ 🐺 *Verdict* 🐺 ~~==~~
Should you get and play this game? Maybe, it's not for everyone. If you're interested in a more reading based game where choices matter that explores the future of privacy, than yes. In case you're not hyped about something like that I would still give the game a go if you can get it on sale

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A fun little document reading simulator.

Seriously, that is the gameplay. It's like a season of 24, where you have to find out where the bomb is going to go off, and it's all up to you, but instead of an elite anti-terrorist agent, you're some rando sitting in front of a PC, hired to sift through documents. That is literally who you are, in the universe of the game. You submit portions of documents to the system, and this unlocks more documents. That may sound a little silly, but the game explains itself pretty well.

No need to worry about 'pixel hunting' or broken logic - all problems are solved and the plot is progressed in all cases by finding the right entry in the right document. If anything, the game holds your hand. 

You can only submit portions of any document that the system deems potentially relevant. You cannot get a game over - you could play this game through by blindly submitting every bit of highlighted text you found, without paying attention to the plot.

But the plot itself is worth paying attention to - a slow-burn story of a parallel world with technology from five minutes into the future. That lawyer guy on youtube who rates the legal accuracy of various pieces of pop culture would probably not rate this thing too highly. But it is fun, and the rationale for everything that happens is internally consistent.

There are branching paths and different outcomes to minor plot points, as well as alternate endings, depending on how you play  - which boils down to which pieces of information you choose to submit or not submit. It is worth the second and even third play-throughs needed to explore every possible outcome.

Which brings me to my two main complaints:

- There is a checkpoint system, limited to the five main chapters/days of the campaign. You can replay a previous day/chapter, but as soon as you start say, chapter two, your progress in the remaining 3 chapters is lost.

- There is no fast-track buttons for voice or text conversations - they play out in real time, complete with 'realistic' pauses, whether you like it or not.

Neither of these are game-breaking, and are more just quality of life features that I found to be conspicuously absent. Their absence mean that secondary playthroughs for achievements/branch discovery take a little longer than they otherwise would.

I bought Orwell on sale, and went in to it without doing much homework, but I got the impression that this would be several distinct yet related cases. It's more like one big ongoing case. Also in contrast to the Ace Attorney games, which Orwell reminds me of just a little, the plot is a little more serious, and the characters a little less colorful. But if you like that series, or sifting through documents to find a terrorist in a dystopian alternate world sounds like fun to you, and if none of what I have written sounds like a deal-breaker, and you find this game at a price that you think is worth ten or so hours of gameplay, go for it.

One final thought - this game is about a surveillance state, but it doesn't take the easy way out. It poses the dilemma of government overreach/corruption for 'safety' vs. privacy/freedom concerns in an interesting way. I would not say that Orwell is quite as brilliant or profound as some of the glowing reviews suggest, but I do like the way that the plot, the gameplay, and the endings you are able to choose all come together to get you thinking about this issue, even if just a little.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A poignant game on the times we live in. I'm a humongous fan of the "Walking Simulator" genre and I stumbled upon this game during the Steam Winter Sale (3 days ago). Orwell has a captivating storyline that takes the "first person" experience quite literally. Without spoiling the game, the story focuses on a user operated software called Orwell, where the player assumes the role as a operator outside the fictatious "Nation", spying on activists that are tagged as potentially violent. 

The user interface is streamlined, dare I say "user-friendly". The fictional profiles depicted in the video game are unnervingly real, pulling me into the experience, as though as I really am spying on others. The characters are well scripted, albeit being scripts of text. The characters are caricatures of stereotypical activists, with complex backgrounds and hidden agendas. 

The "orwellian" connotations that are hinted at in the game are subtle, nuanced without being too overbearing or obvious. As you progressively submit information on labelled targets, you start to feel a heavy burden of responsibility on your shoulders. The multiple options and consequences from submitting false information add more weight to the situation. The activities or rituals performed by the main character are a frighteningly realistic, depecting the state of the world we live in. 

My only complaints include the duration of the game: it is rather short in length, more like a concept game showcasing some of the developer's strengths. The waiting times between each mission is abysmal, sometimes resulting in multiple crashes. 

All in all, this is an underrated gem in the walking simulator category, standing tall with the likes of Gone Home and Soma.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is a dishonest indictment against current surveilance and privacy ethics. It tries to force you into an unethical position so that it can pull off a "gotcha" moment for emotional impact and cheap pedantic morals. You play the nameless analyst that feeds the State with information about people trying to prevent crimes through surveilance of private communications and crossreference of public sources. So far so good. The problems start when the writers remove player agency and predestine outcomes. This happens in two ways.

1) The game uses a system of "conflicting data chunks" which are SUPPOSEDLY contradictory information pieces and you have to judge which is the correct one. Only they aren't. Say that you ram a car in a crossroad in rage. And you do it because you know that this car is going to kill your parents in the next stop. Are these contradictory? Well for this game they are. And you get different outcomes if you select one or the other to "push" to your supervisor. This is called lazy writing and removes player agency. Moving on...

2) You work a narrative case to your best judgement and then the game robs you of an outcome that is as obvious as a billboard on a busy highway. Say that you have a classic crime procedural where the detective is trying to break a suspect. Imagine the detective knows that the suspect is ethical and peaceful and that there is going to be a murder unless the suspect gives up a criminal acquaintance. The expected narrative would be to appeal to humanity and have a reasonable resolution. But no. The game, having known that you did not went for the "cog in the machine" trope, for cheap emo guilt trips, pulls a gotcha and just blows the murder on your face saying you "failed".

At the time of writing this review there is an article in Kotaku about "ludo-narrative dissonance", i.e. how gameplay conflicts with narrative. (link: https://kotaku.com/the-bioshock-problem-when-gameplay-and-narrative-clash-1847698124). This, sometimes can be a good thing as it might shed light into serious ethical conundrums for the player. 
Here the attempt fails because the writers and designers went pedantic and decided to rob the players of even the off chance to experience a story where things would plausibly move in a more nuanced direction than the beat to death pseudo-dilemma "bad state vs bad people" and "security vs freedom". 

Instead of exploring the grey area of these ethics they threw every stereotype in the book to the player and plain and simple punished them when they did not conform to their teenage black and white mentality. 

It's a pity, the review is coming late, but don't bother...

what a SUPERB game!!

I started it just to try it out and give it a go (I got it in the monthly humble) but I found myself so much attached to it I had to finish it all in two sessions!

The game plays out like a detective game, it feels mostly passive because the only thing you can do except reading the events is to gather infos and try to make them as much reliable as possible to the context. the "choice matters" is absolutely present, but at the same time it's not clear when it happens, which is good. no more "the character will remember that" (you hear me telltale??).

There are two things though I disliked. First, what you gather is mostly final, especially with conflicting chunks. I understand what they're doing here, by forcing you to investigate on your own properly before giving out an answer, but sometimes data is ambivalent (one character thinks something, another the opposite with no factual truth in between but just speculation on how you see it) or just ambiguous. Then, when it's uploaded, it's done. Other times you upload things and your advisor jumps to conclusions or take the information literally or completely out of context, some other times they give a background to it. It's very inconsistent and it made me feel "will it understand correctly the meaning of this upload?"

Second, - I will keep it spoiler free - and this one has been a big one for me, there's no neutral ending. At least none that I could find. You can either be the gov's dog by forging evidence, or the rebellious revolutionary that destroyed the system. No in-between. 
This will probably trigger somebody, but I found Orwell a decent tool for investigations, while the whole game continuously point at it as inherently bad, so if you support it you must be bad. I think no tools are good or bad, it's how we use them and we can see it in this game the ethical modifications done to it have improved it by far. It has flaws, true, (especially if you give the tool to an untrained person treating it as a game... what the heck, seriously.) but all in all if the system is actually restricted to investigate actual threats it could be an interesting way to manage it. We all had to deal with terrorists lately unfortunately, and we all cry for help and for prevention. This might be another tool to help us. 

So I don't get why you HAVE to be bad if you support it? Why can't you just incriminate the bombers and call it a day? why do you need to fabricate evidence or else being called disobedient and incriminate yourself? Very bummed by this choice in the climax of the ending.

This game is a thought-provoking foray into the concept of the Orwellian panopticon of many distopian fiction.  It cronicles the choices that you, as an investigator, make in the resolution of a terrorism investigation.  If you enjoy games like [u]Papers, Please[/u] and Telltale Games' [u]Wolf Among Us[/u], you'll definitely like this game.  I had doubts about the tesselated graphics (they are remeniscent of the original  [u]Flashback[/u]), but they primarily only serve as avatars in the web-of-knowledge that you construct as part of the investigation.

Some have complained about the idea of the game being...simplistic; however, the game seems to have a decent number of branches depending on which of the pieces of intel you select and (importantly) [i]when you select them[/i].  I haven't begun to explore all of the nodes of the decision tree, but with each of the paths that I've traversed I only want to know more of the story.  Is there an ultimate [b]truth[/b]?  I must know.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a thought-provoking game that successfully delves into the complex world of surveillance and privacy, raising numerous ethical questions and dilemmas. Its core premise, which involves taking on the role of a government operative monitoring citizens' digital lives, is both innovative and unsettling. It challenges players to balance national security with personal privacy, making every decision carry significant weight and moral ambiguity.

Gameplay Mechanics

The mechanics are straightforward, primarily revolving around reading through documents, chat logs, and social media posts to piece together clues about potential threats. While this simplicity makes the game accessible, it can also lead to a repetitive and tedious experience. The process of sifting through information often lacks variety, and the gameplay can become monotonous over time. Moreover, the game's interface, although intuitive, sometimes suffers from minor bugs that can force you to reload the Game. There are also some minor instances where progression is unclear, leaving players uncertain about their next steps.

Narrative and Storytelling

One of the strengths of Orwell lies in its narrative, which includes several compelling plot twists that keep the player engaged. The story explores themes of power, trust, and the consequences of unchecked surveillance, offering moments of genuine intrigue and suspense. However, despite these high points, the overall plot can feel somewhat bland and unremarkable by the conclusion. The characters, while initially interesting, sometimes lack depth, and the story does not always capitalize on its potential to deliver a truly memorable experience.

Ethical Themes and Impact

Where Orwell truly shines is in its exploration of ethical issues. The game does not shy away from presenting the moral complexities of surveillance, forcing players to confront the impact of their actions on individuals' lives. This aspect of the game is its most compelling feature, prompting players to reflect on real-world implications and the delicate balance between security and privacy.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a game with a powerful concept that effectively engages with important ethical themes. Its simple mechanics can become repetitive, and minor technical issues can hinder the experience. While the narrative has strong moments, it ultimately falls short of being truly remarkable. Nevertheless, the game’s exploration of surveillance and privacy makes it a worthwhile experience for those interested in thought-provoking and socially relevant games.

- Innovative and unsettling premise
- Compelling plot twists
- Intuitive interface

Cons:

- Repetitive and tedious mechanics
- Minor bugs and progression issues
- Overall bland and unremarkable plot
- Characters lack depth

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]TL:DR: [/b] Does 1984 ring a bell? Yes? You are all good, skip this. No? Block off four hours and prepare a lighthearted movie after to flush the existential horror.

[h1]What is Orwell?[/h1]
The player takes the role of an independent third party taking the reigns of the most powerful surveillance technology ever built tasked with the investigation of a terrorist attack on a monument in the capital of a fictitious country called The Nation. Armed with a context sensitive browser the player dives head first into one medium deep rabbit hole.

[h1]Game Design | The Awesome (+2)[/h1]
I adore the brutalist functionality of the game design. It feels like a desk job. There is nothing special to it. Everything works as one would expect it to. It should feel cold. It should provide a degree of separation from the subject while not hindering gameplay. This is one of the hardest tricks any game designer can pull off. Take it from a boring person who unironically loves to create spreadsheets for any number of things. This [i]rocks[/i].

[h1]Audio design | The Terrible (-2)[/h1]
Coming in on the opposite side of the spectrum is audio design. Or lack thereof. The only notable attempt at anything are dynamic music changes when the player comes across [i]shocking[/i] new information. And yes, I am exaggerating, because the music is exaggerating. The whiplash from the norm is that great. It arrives suddenly and leaves before it had a chance to order a frickin' latte. Then there are all the missed opportunities. The player has access to various types of data from texts, to web pages, to voice calls. Instead of a transcript it would have been great to have the few calls fully voiced. It would have brought the player even closer to the characters.

[h1]Characters | The Bad (-1)[/h1]
...of which Orwell utilizes several one dimensional archetypes with a couple of exceptions that show a hint of a second dimension. Fortunately for the game, the player is not forced to linger on any of the cast. We get just as much as we need to understand from where the wind is blowing before moving on to the next person. For better or worse, commentary on surveillance killing the human experience acts as the main character of the game and is largely responsible for the ankle deep depth of the human pawns.

[h1]Closing Thoughts | The Adequate (0)[/h1]
Orwell is a tricky proposition. On one side it is concise, excellently showcases pitfalls of absolute surveillance and should be a mandatory play on any high school, on the other side it is cynical to the core and does not allow a solution of the privacy/security conundrum. I could speculate that the original intention of the authors was to show the only winning move is not to play. However, I am writing this script seven years after the release in a world that is inching closer and closer to a world of AI driven absolute surveillance. The absolute surveillance of Orwell fails even with a human at the helm of its moral compass, what chance do we have in the real world without such an agent? At the end of the day art is a reflection of our perceived reality. I understand that having no way out nets a more chilling experience. However, if the resolution does not provide a positive outlook, something to aspire to, it leaves the observer in a very dark place.

[hr][/hr]

[h4]Note[/h4]
Individual sections (and the whole game) are critiqued on a scale of [i]The Terrible (-2)[/i] from the worse to [i]The Awesome (+2)[/i].

review_text_raw:
Orwell is a small indie game that may or may not be good based on what kinds of games the player may enjoy. I will be reviewing the game with a pro/ con style and end with my conclusion.

Pro:
     The story is very deep. Imagine watching a murder mystery show, there is alot of plot twists that really makes you wonder things like who really did it since everyone looks guilty. The story is shaped based on the player's decisions on what they consider important or facts. From there the response might be different based on the players decisions.

       Good ambient music. The music is not much but at times it does emphasis the mood that is suppose to be potrayed. In a moment where you discover something shocking the music will change to potray a shocking mood.

        The art is very simplistic. That is not a bad thing by any stretch of the imagination. It is again an indie game but it does remind me of the polygon designs of super hot and that was a decent looking game. The main point is that the visuals do not overly distract the player  from important moments of the game. It allows for a more cleaner visual naritive with it's simplistic design.

Con:
      The game has a few bugs. The main one I faced was moments that the game froze requiring me to ALT+F4 to close the game and continue where I left off. At moments it is possible for the game to have a dialogue box open but on the background there will be an ongoing conversation via texting or calling and it would prevent you from scrolling through the text to properly read it. This is very likely to happen towards the end of the game.

Conclusion:
         The game is pretty good. The stroy did throw me through a few loops. I did not expect a few of these plot twists and playing through the game was exciting to see how the story played out. Unfortunantly replaying is not nearly as great since the story changes are pretty minor at points and lack any worth wild plot twists when going down a different branching path. Ultimatly  I would reccomend this game but mainly to people who enjoy games with a pretty rich story and branching plot decisions like walking dead.

review_text_raw:
I really want to like Orwell for the principle of trying to deliver a social media exploitation simulator, but ultimately, it's a flow-chart puzzle that only allows the player to progress once he or she has collected the necessary datachunks. This would be unobtrusive if the narrator (the guide) wasn't hovering over you at all times like an incompetent manager - instantly responding with positive or negative feedback. The game would be much better if you could upload information to something like a holding pool to review as a whole before submitting it to something like a file or record for the manager to review, but instead, the game flow pauses and continues with no continuity of real-time, even though the game desperately tries to emulate this moment of your day on the job . You might have a hunch about a suspect as you read information, so you would think to point out correlated characteristics, but nope, that doesn't matter because you can only upload information the game has already marked as valid.

Orwell is unique and immersive, so it does have that going for it, but the flow-chart progression heavily relies on the game being bug free. I hit a bug/glitch/design flaw in the second episode in which a datachunk in the suspects relationship field was not registering that I uploaded it. As a result, I was stuck. I poured over every bit of information for about three hours before I finally searched online for help and wound up uploading conflicting datachunks to do what I thought would fail the mission, but oh, how convenient, the game saves the day by holding my hand and progressing anyway. So, it’s more like an interactive novel than a social-engineering investigation simulator.

I really wanted to like this, but after multiple attempts, I still cannot get past day 3. There are various reports of a game-breaking bug that blocks access to critical parts of the game, preventing any progress.

Further, there are inexplicable logic errors that prevent certain information being extracted earlier than the game expects, and cases where obvious information doesn't seem to be usable at-all (such as profile pictures for certain people). It makes the experience inconsistent and frustrating.

So, more disappointing than fulfilling.
